title: "Stochastic differential equations"
description: "How to add noise to a differential equation without angering the mathematicians: an ensemble of sample paths, the Euler–Maruyama scheme, and the odd rule that noise scales with the square root of the time step."
toc: true
execute:

---

Almost every model I work with has noise in it. Synaptic input arrives at
irregular times, spontaneous activity in the cortex fluctuates, and even a
tidy rate model gets a noise term the moment it is compared with data. The
usual way to write this down is to take an ordinary differential equation and
add a random forcing term. That looks harmless, and in practice it mostly is,
but the step from "add noise" to "a stochastic differential equation" hides a
few genuine surprises. In 2022 I gave a short talk about these at our lab's
coffee meeting under the title "How to avoid angering the mathematicians".
The first figure grows a bundle of sample paths while you watch, and the
second lets you break the simulation on purpose by picking the wrong time
step.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
// shared helpers: one persistent canvas per explorable, text-sized fonts, responsive width
exFont = ({size: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontSize, family: getComputedStyle(document.body).fontFamily, toString() { return this.size + " " + this.family; }})
exFg = () => getComputedStyle(document.body).color
mkCanvas = (W, H) => {
  const c = DOM.context2d(W, H);
  c.canvas.style.width = "100%"; c.canvas.style.maxWidth = W + "px"; c.canvas.style.height = "auto";
  return c;
}
axisBox = (c, x, y, w, h) => { c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeRect(x, y, w, h); }
```

## From a spring to a random walk

My talk started with a spring, because that is where the trouble starts. A
mass on a damped spring, pushed by an external force $w(t)$, obeys

$$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \gamma\,\frac{dx}{dt} + \nu^2 x = w(t),$$

with $x$ the position, $\gamma$ the damping and $\nu$ the natural frequency.
This is a second-order linear ordinary differential equation, and everything
about it is well understood: it has exactly one solution for a given start,
and you can find it by hand or with a standard numerical scheme such as Euler
or Runge–Kutta. Now let the force be random. The natural choice is white
noise, a process $w(t)$ that has zero mean, is Gaussian, and whose values at
any two different times are independent. The spring is now a stochastic
differential equation, and the textbook guarantees no longer apply.

The reason is that white noise is a strange object. Independence at every
pair of times means it is discontinuous everywhere, and it takes arbitrarily
large values in any interval, however short. The theory of ordinary
differential equations asks for a continuous right-hand side, so the usual
existence and uniqueness theorem cannot even be stated, and the integral
$\int w(t)\,dt$ that would give the solution does not exist as an ordinary
integral because $w$ is unbounded. The way out is to stop talking about $w$
and talk instead about its running sum, Brownian motion $\beta(t)$. Brownian
motion is continuous, so integrals against its increments $d\beta$ can be
made to work. Formally $w = d\beta/dt$, but $\beta$ has no derivative
anywhere, which is exactly why $w$ is so badly behaved. This is the origin of
Itô calculus, and it is also why its chain rule has an extra term that the
ordinary one does not: a tiny increment $d\beta$ is not negligible when
squared, because $(d\beta)^2$ behaves like $dt$. All of this is why a
mathematician winces when $w(t)$ is written into an equation as if it were an
ordinary function. The mathematics allows the equation, as long as you say
what you mean by the integral.

The name "white noise", by the way, comes from the spectrum. By the
Wiener–Khinchin theorem (Wiener 1930; Khintchine 1934), the power spectrum
of a stationary process is the Fourier transform of its autocorrelation,
and the delta-shaped autocorrelation of $w$ transforms into a flat spectrum,
all frequencies present in equal measure, as in white light. Brownian
motion, the running sum of white noise, has a spectrum that falls as
$1/f^2$ and is called brown noise, after the motion rather than the colour,
and the $1/f$ spectrum in between is pink. That deserves a page of its own,
and it is on the list.

The two equations on this page are the ones you are most likely to meet.
Written in the Itô form, they are

$$\text{Brownian motion:}\qquad dx = D\, d\beta$$

$$\text{Ornstein–Uhlenbeck:}\qquad dx = -\theta\, x\, dt + D\, d\beta .$$

The first is a random walk: $x$ wanders with no preference for any value and
spreads out forever, which is also the equation for the position of a
diffusing particle. The second adds a spring that pulls $x$ back towards
zero with rate $\theta$, so the wandering is kept in check. The
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process (Uhlenbeck and Ornstein 1930) was invented for the
velocity of a Brownian particle, and it is the standard model for anything
that fluctuates around a set point, from membrane potentials to interest
rates. The third option in the figure is the noisy spring itself, with
$\nu = 2$ fixed and the slider setting the damping $\gamma$. Written as a
first-order system in position and velocity it is

$$\text{Noisy spring:}\qquad dx = v\, dt, \qquad dv = (-\gamma\, v - \nu^2 x)\, dt + D\, d\beta .$$

Because these equations are linear, their solutions can be described
completely. The whole ensemble of possible paths is Gaussian at every time,
with a mean that follows the noise-free equation and a variance that grows in
a known way. Starting from $x_0$, Brownian motion has mean $x_0$ and variance
$D^2 t$, so its spread grows without limit as $\sqrt{t}$. The
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process has mean $x_0 e^{-\theta t}$ and variance
$\frac{D^2}{2\theta}\left(1 - e^{-2\theta t}\right)$, which settles at
$D^2/(2\theta)$. The first figure draws these formulas over the simulated
ensemble, so you can check them.

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sdModel = Inputs.radio(new Map([["Brownian motion", "bm"], ["Ornstein–Uhlenbeck", "ou"], ["Noisy spring", "spring"]]), {value: "ou", label: "Model"})
viewof sdTheta = Inputs.range([0.1, 3], {value: 1, step: 0.1, label: "θ (pull towards 0; damping γ for the spring)"})
viewof sdD = Inputs.range([0, 2], {value: 1, step: 0.05, label: "D (noise strength)"})
viewof sdPause = Inputs.toggle({label: "Pause"})
viewof sdReset = Inputs.button("Restart")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sdRandn = () => {
  let u = 0, v = 0;
  while (u === 0) u = Math.random();
  while (v === 0) v = Math.random();
  return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * v);
}
sdPar = ({T: 10, dt: 0.01, N: 300, show: 12, x0: 2, nu: 2})
sdState = {
  sdReset;
  const model = sdModel, theta = sdTheta, D = sdD;
  const {T, dt, N, show, x0, nu} = sdPar, n = Math.round(T / dt) + 1;
  const x = new Float32Array(N).fill(x0), v = new Float32Array(N);
  const traces = Array.from({length: show}, () => new Float32Array(n).fill(x0));
  const mean = new Float32Array(n).fill(x0), sd = new Float32Array(n);
  let k = 0;
  const sq = Math.sqrt(dt);
  while (true) {
    if (!viewof sdPause.value && k < n - 1) {
      for (let s = 0; s < 5 && k < n - 1; s++) {
        k++;
        let sum = 0, sum2 = 0;
        for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
          const db = sdRandn() * sq;
          if (model === "bm") x[i] += D * db;
          else if (model === "ou") x[i] += -theta * x[i] * dt + D * db;
          else { const a = -theta * v[i] - nu * nu * x[i]; x[i] += v[i] * dt; v[i] += a * dt + D * db; }
          sum += x[i]; sum2 += x[i] * x[i];
        }
        for (let j = 0; j < show; j++) traces[j][k] = x[j];
        mean[k] = sum / N; sd[k] = Math.sqrt(Math.max(0, sum2 / N - mean[k] * mean[k]));
      }
    }
    yield {x, traces, mean, sd, k, t: k * dt, model, theta, D};
  }
}
sdTheory = (model, theta, D, t, x0) => {
  if (model === "bm") return {m: x0, s: D * Math.sqrt(t)};
  if (model === "ou") return {m: x0 * Math.exp(-theta * t), s: D * Math.sqrt((1 - Math.exp(-2 * theta * t)) / (2 * theta))};
  return null;
}
sdCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 370)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const st = sdState, c = sdCanvas, fg = exFg(), W = 760, H = 370;
  const {T, dt, N, x0} = sdPar, ymax = 5;
  const P = {x0: 56, y0: 14, w: 500, h: 270}, R = {x0: 590, y0: 14, w: 150, h: 270};
  const sx = t => P.x0 + P.w * t / T, sy = v => P.y0 + P.h * (1 - (v + ymax) / (2 * ymax));
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  // left: sample paths with ensemble band
  axisBox(c, P.x0, P.y0, P.w, P.h);
  c.save(); c.beginPath(); c.rect(P.x0, P.y0, P.w, P.h); c.clip();
  c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.setLineDash([3, 4]); c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(P.x0, sy(0)); c.lineTo(P.x0 + P.w, sy(0)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  c.fillStyle = "rgba(31,119,180,0.18)"; c.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i <= st.k; i++) c.lineTo(sx(i * dt), sy(st.mean[i] + st.sd[i]));
  for (let i = st.k; i >= 0; i--) c.lineTo(sx(i * dt), sy(st.mean[i] - st.sd[i]));
  c.closePath(); c.fill();
  c.lineWidth = 1; c.strokeStyle = "#ff7f0e"; c.globalAlpha = 0.6;
  for (const tr of st.traces) { c.beginPath(); for (let i = 0; i <= st.k; i++) i ? c.lineTo(sx(i * dt), sy(tr[i])) : c.moveTo(sx(0), sy(tr[0])); c.stroke(); }
  c.globalAlpha = 1; c.lineWidth = 2.5; c.strokeStyle = "#1f77b4"; c.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i <= st.k; i++) i ? c.lineTo(sx(i * dt), sy(st.mean[i])) : c.moveTo(sx(0), sy(st.mean[0]));
  c.stroke();
  const th = sdTheory(st.model, st.theta, st.D, 0, x0);
  if (th) {
    c.strokeStyle = fg; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.setLineDash([6, 4]);
    for (const sgn of [1, -1]) { c.beginPath(); for (let i = 0; i <= st.k; i++) { const q = sdTheory(st.model, st.theta, st.D, i * dt, x0); i ? c.lineTo(sx(i * dt), sy(q.m + sgn * q.s)) : c.moveTo(sx(0), sy(q.m)); } c.stroke(); }
    c.setLineDash([]);
  }
  c.restore();
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText("time t", P.x0 + P.w / 2, P.y0 + P.h + 26); c.fillText("0", sx(0), P.y0 + P.h + 26); c.fillText(T, sx(T), P.y0 + P.h + 26);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("x", P.x0 - 12, P.y0 + P.h / 2 - 16);
  for (const yv of [-ymax, 0, ymax]) c.fillText(yv, P.x0 - 8, sy(yv) + 5);
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText(`t = ${st.t.toFixed(1)}`, P.x0 + 8, P.y0 + 20);
  // right: histogram of x across the ensemble at time t, with the predicted Gaussian
  axisBox(c, R.x0, R.y0, R.w, R.h);
  const nb = 40, bins = new Float32Array(nb), bw = 2 * ymax / nb;
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { const b = Math.floor((st.x[i] + ymax) / bw); if (b >= 0 && b < nb) bins[b]++; }
  const dens = Array.from(bins, b => b / (N * bw));
  const m = st.mean[st.k], s = st.sd[st.k];
  const q = th ? sdTheory(st.model, st.theta, st.D, st.t, x0) : {m, s};
  const peak = 1.15 * Math.max(...dens, q.s > 1e-3 ? 1 / (q.s * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)) : 0, 0.05);
  const rx = d => R.x0 + R.w * Math.min(1, d / peak);
  c.fillStyle = "rgba(255,127,14,0.55)";
  for (let b = 0; b < nb; b++) { const lo = -ymax + b * bw; c.fillRect(R.x0, sy(lo + bw), rx(dens[b]) - R.x0, sy(lo) - sy(lo + bw)); }
  if (q.s > 1e-3) {
    c.save(); c.beginPath(); c.rect(R.x0, R.y0, R.w, R.h); c.clip();
    c.strokeStyle = fg; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.setLineDash([6, 4]); c.beginPath();
    for (let i = 0; i <= 100; i++) { const yv = -ymax + 2 * ymax * i / 100, d = Math.exp(-0.5 * ((yv - q.m) / q.s) ** 2) / (q.s * Math.sqrt(2 * Math.PI)); i ? c.lineTo(rx(d), sy(yv)) : c.moveTo(rx(d), sy(yv)); }
    c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]); c.restore();
  }
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center"; c.fillText("x at time t", R.x0 + R.w / 2, R.y0 + R.h + 26);
  c.textAlign = "left";
  c.fillText(`mean ${m.toFixed(2)}`, R.x0 + 6, R.y0 + 20);
  c.fillText(`std ${s.toFixed(2)}`, R.x0 + 6, R.y0 + 38);
  if (th) c.fillText(`formula ${q.s.toFixed(2)}`, R.x0 + 6, R.y0 + 56);
  // legend below the axes
  let lx = P.x0, ly = P.y0 + P.h + 50;
  for (const [txt, col] of [["orange: sample paths", "#ff7f0e"], ["blue: ensemble mean", "#1f77b4"], ["band: mean ± 1 std", "#1f77b4"], ["dashed: formula", fg]]) {
    c.fillStyle = col; c.fillText(txt, lx, ly); lx += c.measureText(txt).width + 16;
  }
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Solving them numerically

Most of the time nobody solves these equations by hand. The simplest scheme is
Euler–Maruyama, which is the Euler method with one change. For an equation
$dx = f(x)\,dt + L(x)\,d\beta$ it reads

$$x_{k+1} = x_k + f(x_k)\,\Delta t + L(x_k)\,\Delta\beta_k, \qquad
\Delta\beta_k \sim \mathcal N(0, \Delta t),$$

so each step adds a Gaussian random number with variance $\Delta t$, or
equivalently a standard normal number multiplied by $\sqrt{\Delta t}$. That
square root is the whole point. If you treat the noise like any other term
and multiply it by $\Delta t$, the random part shrinks faster than the
deterministic part as the step gets smaller, and in the limit it vanishes.
Put differently, multiplying the noise by $\Delta t$ is the same as running
Euler–Maruyama with a noise strength $D\sqrt{\Delta t}$: the scheme is
internally consistent, but it solves a different equation, and which one
depends on the time step. The second figure shows this directly.
Higher-order schemes exist, Milstein
being the most common, but for the models on this page Euler–Maruyama with a
small step is all you need.


```{ojs}
//| echo: false
viewof sdDt = Inputs.radio([5, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01], {value: 0.1, label: "Δt", format: d => String(d)})
viewof sdRedraw = Inputs.button("New noise")
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
sdDtSteps = [5, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01]
sdDtSpread = (dt, scale, N, T, D) => {
  const n = Math.round(T / dt); let sum2 = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) { let x = 0; for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) x += D * sdRandn() * scale; sum2 += x * x; }
  return Math.sqrt(sum2 / N);
}
sdDtSweep = {
  sdRedraw;
  const T = 10, D = 1, N = 500;
  return sdDtSteps.map(dt => ({dt, sqrt: sdDtSpread(dt, Math.sqrt(dt), N, T, D), lin: sdDtSpread(dt, dt, N, T, D)}));
}
sdDtRun = {
  sdRedraw;
  const T = 10, D = 1, N = 500, show = 15, dt = sdDt, n = Math.round(T / dt);
  const out = {};
  for (const [key, scale] of [["sqrt", Math.sqrt(dt)], ["lin", dt]]) {
    const paths = Array.from({length: show}, () => [0]);
    let sum2 = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
      let x = 0;
      for (let k = 0; k < n; k++) { x += D * sdRandn() * scale; if (i < show) paths[i].push(x); }
      sum2 += x * x;
    }
    out[key] = {paths, std: Math.sqrt(sum2 / N)};
  }
  return {...out, dt, T, D, exact: D * Math.sqrt(T)};
}
sdDtCanvas = mkCanvas(760, 352)
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
{
  const r = sdDtRun, sw = sdDtSweep, c = sdDtCanvas, fg = exFg(), W = 760, H = 352, ymax = 8;
  const blue = "#1f77b4", orange = "#ff7f0e";
  c.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); c.font = exFont;
  const panels = [
    {key: "sqrt", x0: 56, title: "noise × √Δt (Euler–Maruyama)", col: blue},
    {key: "lin", x0: 300, title: "noise × Δt (naive Euler)", col: orange}
  ];
  for (const p of panels) {
    const P = {x0: p.x0, y0: 14, w: 200, h: 230}, run = r[p.key], n = run.paths[0].length - 1;
    const sx = i => P.x0 + P.w * i / n, sy = v => P.y0 + P.h * (1 - (v + ymax) / (2 * ymax));
    axisBox(c, P.x0, P.y0, P.w, P.h);
    c.save(); c.beginPath(); c.rect(P.x0, P.y0, P.w, P.h); c.clip();
    c.strokeStyle = "#999"; c.setLineDash([3, 4]); c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(P.x0, sy(0)); c.lineTo(P.x0 + P.w, sy(0)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
    c.strokeStyle = p.col; c.lineWidth = 1; c.globalAlpha = 0.7;
    for (const path of run.paths) { c.beginPath(); path.forEach((v, i) => i ? c.lineTo(sx(i), sy(v)) : c.moveTo(sx(0), sy(v))); c.stroke(); }
    c.globalAlpha = 1; c.strokeStyle = fg; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.setLineDash([6, 4]);
    for (const sgn of [1, -1]) { c.beginPath(); for (let i = 0; i <= 50; i++) { const t = r.T * i / 50; i ? c.lineTo(P.x0 + P.w * i / 50, sy(sgn * r.D * Math.sqrt(t))) : c.moveTo(P.x0, sy(0)); } c.stroke(); }
    c.setLineDash([]); c.restore();
    c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
    c.fillText("time t", P.x0 + P.w / 2, P.y0 + P.h + 26); c.fillText("0", P.x0, P.y0 + P.h + 26); c.fillText(r.T, P.x0 + P.w, P.y0 + P.h + 26);
    c.fillStyle = p.col; c.fillText(p.title, P.x0 + P.w / 2, P.y0 + P.h + 48);
    c.fillStyle = fg; c.fillText(`spread at t = ${r.T}: ${run.std.toFixed(2)}`, P.x0 + P.w / 2, P.y0 + P.h + 70);
  }
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillStyle = fg; for (const yv of [-ymax, 0, ymax]) c.fillText(yv, 56 - 8, 14 + 230 * (1 - (yv + ymax) / (2 * ymax)) + 5);
  c.fillText("x", 56 - 12, 14 + 115 - 16);
  // convergence panel: spread at t = T against Δt for both schemes
  const Cv = {x0: 560, y0: 14, w: 184, h: 230}, smax = 8;
  const lx = dt => Cv.x0 + Cv.w * (Math.log10(dt) + 2) / 3, ly = sd => Cv.y0 + Cv.h * (1 - sd / smax);
  axisBox(c, Cv.x0, Cv.y0, Cv.w, Cv.h);
  c.strokeStyle = fg; c.lineWidth = 1.5; c.setLineDash([6, 4]); c.beginPath(); c.moveTo(Cv.x0, ly(r.exact)); c.lineTo(Cv.x0 + Cv.w, ly(r.exact)); c.stroke(); c.setLineDash([]);
  for (const [key, col] of [["sqrt", blue], ["lin", orange]]) {
    c.strokeStyle = col; c.lineWidth = 1; c.beginPath(); sw.forEach((q, i) => i ? c.lineTo(lx(q.dt), ly(q[key])) : c.moveTo(lx(q.dt), ly(q[key]))); c.stroke();
    c.fillStyle = col; for (const q of sw) { c.beginPath(); c.arc(lx(q.dt), ly(q[key]), q.dt === r.dt ? 6 : 3.5, 0, 2 * Math.PI); c.fill(); }
  }
  c.fillStyle = fg; c.textAlign = "center";
  c.fillText("Δt (log scale)", Cv.x0 + Cv.w / 2, Cv.y0 + Cv.h + 26);
  for (const d of [0.01, 0.1, 1, 10]) c.fillText(String(d), lx(d), Cv.y0 + Cv.h + 46);
  c.fillText(`spread at t = ${r.T}`, Cv.x0 + Cv.w / 2, Cv.y0 + Cv.h + 70);
  c.textAlign = "right"; c.fillText("0", Cv.x0 - 6, ly(0) + 5); c.fillText(smax, Cv.x0 - 6, ly(smax) + 5); c.fillText(`√${r.T}`, Cv.x0 - 6, ly(r.exact) + 5);
  c.textAlign = "left"; c.fillText("dashed: exact spread √t", 56, H - 10);
  return c.canvas;
}
```

## Reading the figure

In the first figure, the panel on the left shows twelve sample paths in
orange, all started at $x_0 = 2$ and simulated with Euler–Maruyama at
$\Delta t = 0.01$. Behind them, the blue line is the mean of a larger
ensemble of 300 paths and the blue band is that ensemble's mean plus and minus
one standard deviation, as the legend under the panel says. The dashed black lines are the formulas for the
Brownian and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck cases, mean plus and minus one standard
deviation, so when the simulation is right the band and the dashed lines
should agree up to sampling noise. The noisy spring has no dashed lines; its
ensemble statistics would need a longer formula, and the band speaks for
itself.

The panel on the right is a histogram of where the 300 paths are at the
current moment, turned on its side so that it shares the vertical axis with
the paths. The dashed curve is the Gaussian predicted by the formulas, or, for
the spring, the Gaussian with the ensemble's own mean and standard deviation.
The three numbers above it are the ensemble mean, the ensemble standard
deviation and the predicted standard deviation. The histogram is rescaled
to fit its panel, so compare widths along the vertical axis, not bar
lengths. Changing a slider or the model restarts the simulation from
$t = 0$.

The second figure runs the same random walk, $dx = d\beta$ with $D = 1$, twice
with the time step you choose. On the left each step adds a standard normal
number times $\sqrt{\Delta t}$, on the right the same number times
$\Delta t$. The dashed lines in both panels are the same thing, the exact
spread $\sqrt{t}$ of the equation being solved, and the number under each
panel is the measured standard deviation of 500 paths at $t = 10$. The third
panel collects that number for every available time step, blue for
Euler–Maruyama and orange for naive Euler, against the exact value $\sqrt{10}
\approx 3.16$ as a dashed line, with the current time step drawn larger.

## Things to try

Start with the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process at the default values. The mean
decays from 2 towards 0 with time constant $1/\theta$, and the band widens
until it reaches a standard deviation of $D/\sqrt{2\theta}$, which is 0.71
for the defaults. Once the mean has settled, the histogram on the right stops
changing shape even though every individual path keeps moving. That is the
stationary distribution, and it is what people mean when they say that
an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process "has" a variance. Raise $\theta$ and the band
narrows and settles faster. Lower it and the process starts to look like
Brownian motion for a while before the pull makes itself felt.

Switch to Brownian motion. Now nothing pulls $x$ back, the mean stays at 2
and the band keeps growing as $\sqrt t$, reaching a standard deviation of
$D\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ for $D = 1$ at the end of the run. The histogram
just keeps flattening. Set $D$ to 2 and watch how many paths leave the plot:
the standard deviation at $t = 10$ is now 6.3, well beyond the axis.

Switch to the noisy spring. With $\gamma = 1$ the mean oscillates a few times
before it dies away, and the band is narrower than for the
Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process at the same $D$, because the noise drives the
velocity rather than the position and the spring filters it. Set the damping
to 0.1 and the paths ring at the natural frequency for the whole run, still
roughly in step with each other, while the mean decays only slowly and the
band widens a little with every swing. Ten time units is too short to see
where this ends up, but the trend is the point: the noise slowly knocks the
paths out of phase with one another, so over a long enough run the mean
fades away while every single path keeps oscillating. The ensemble mean is
then a poor description of any member of the ensemble, which is worth
remembering whenever a model is compared with trial-averaged data.

In the second figure, begin with $\Delta t = 1$. The two path panels are
indistinguishable, because $\sqrt{1} = 1$, and the two dots in the third
panel coincide on the dashed line. Go the other way first, to $\Delta t = 2$
and then 5. With only five steps in the whole run the paths are crude in
both panels, but the blue spread stays near 3.2 while the orange one climbs
to 4.5 and then 7.1: a coarse step overstates the noise in the naive scheme
just as a fine step understates it. Now reduce the step. The left panel stays
the same apart from looking smoother, and its spread stays near 3.2 at every
step: the blue dots sit on the line. The right panel shrinks. Its paths
still spread as $\sqrt t$, since it is a random walk like any other, only
one with a weaker noise, and the spread at $t = 10$ drops to 1.0 at
$\Delta t = 0.1$ and 0.32 at $\Delta t = 0.01$. The orange dots fall away
from the line as $\sqrt{\Delta t}$. A numerical scheme is supposed to give
an answer that stops depending on $\Delta t$ once the step is small enough,
and the naive one never does. In the limit of a vanishing step its noise
would disappear altogether. This is the practical face of everything in the
section on white noise. A random force that leaves a finite mark in a finite
time must have an infinite amplitude in the limit, and the $\sqrt{\Delta t}$
in the Euler–Maruyama scheme is the bookkeeping that makes that work on a
computer. If a simulation of a noisy model gives results that change when
you refine the time step, this is the first thing to check.

This page follows my 2022 coffee-meeting talk, which drew mostly on the
lecture notes by Särkkä (2012), since published as a book (Särkkä and Solin
2019). Higham (2001) is the friendliest introduction to the numerical side
and the source of the Euler–Maruyama figure in the talk. A disclaimer is in
order: I once tried studying mathematics alongside biophysics and gave it
up in favour of the physics part of my degree, so the mathematicians in the
title may be angered by this page after all. If you are one of them, Särkkä and Solin (2019) has the proper
version.

## Numerical details

Both figures use the Euler–Maruyama scheme exactly as written above, with
standard normal numbers from the Box–Muller transform. The first figure
integrates 300 paths with $\Delta t = 0.01$ from $x_0 = 2$ (and $v_0 = 0$
for the spring) to $T = 10$, draws 12 of them, and computes the mean and
standard deviation across all 300 at every step; the spring uses $\nu = 2$.
The second figure integrates 500 paths of $dx = d\beta$ with $D = 1$ to
$T = 10$ at the chosen $\Delta t$ and draws 15 of them; the convergence
panel repeats the 500-path run for each of the nine available time steps
with both schemes. The naive Euler
scheme, with the noise increment multiplied by $\Delta t$ instead of
$\sqrt{\Delta t}$, is used nowhere except in the right panel of that
figure, where it is the point.
